documents.title: Code of Academic Integrity
documents.summary: One sentence of the Code of Academic Integrity's cheating standard makes AI-generated work not the student's own and not permitted unless the instructor expressly says so. The rest of the long Code is not AI-specific, and no AI-specific procedures, disclosure rules or penalties are given.
documents.stance_why: The Code says "Work generated by artificial intelligence is not considered to be created by the student and is not permitted unless expressly stated by the instructor." AI is banned unless explicitly permitted, which is restrict, not delegates, because the default is a ban.

units.why: The cheating standard says "Work generated by artificial intelligence is not considered to be created by the student and is not permitted unless expressly stated by the instructor." That is a default ban with an instructor exception, so it is a fallback rule (P06) rather than a plain prohibition; P01 was not chosen because the exception is the point of the sentence.
units.anchor: be created by the student and is not permitted unless expressly stated by the instructor.

units.why: The sentence "Students may not claim as their own work any portion of academic work that was not created by the student" binds students to submit only their own work, which is an ownership rule (P29) and is the premise that makes AI-generated work count as cheating.
units.anchor: Students may not claim as their own work any portion of academic work that was

units.why: "Students may only use materials approved by their instructor when completing an assignment or exam" puts the permission decision with the instructor, so it fits P04; the AI-specific sentence is coded separately.
units.anchor: Students may only use materials approved by their instructor when completing an assignment or exam.
units.fit_note: Not AI-specific; it covers all materials, which includes AI tools by implication.

units.why: "Students must adhere to the guidelines for completing academic work provided by their instructors, Exam Proctoring Center staff, or other entities overseeing academic work" makes students follow whoever oversees the work; this is students learning and following the rules that apply (P78), not a ban.
units.anchor: Students must adhere to the guidelines for completing academic work provided by their instructors
units.fit_note: General academic-work guidelines, not AI-specific.

units.why: "Violations of this standard constitute cheating" follows the AI sentence in the same standard, so unauthorized AI-generated work is classed as cheating (P36). No penalty is stated here, so P37 does not apply.
units.anchor: Violations of this standard constitute cheating.

documents.title: About AI at UVM
documents.summary: A short university AI site page that defines AI terms and lists advisory considerations on integrity, privacy, transparency, ethics and ongoing learning. It sets no rules or bans and welcomes AI use with transparency and care.
documents.stance_why: The page says AI "is a powerful tool that can be used for learning, productivity, and creativity" and asks for transparency, so use is allowed with soft conditions. It does not hand decisions to instructors or ban anything, so permit rather than delegates.

units.why: The Definitions section defines AI, generative AI and AI agents; its text "Generative AI encompasses models and systems designed to produce novel content" sets what the site's guidance covers (P61).
units.anchor: Generative AI encompasses models and systems designed to produce novel content, such as text, images,

units.why: "Being transparent about when and how you use AI tools, such as ChatGPT, can help maintain trust and clarity in academic work" is advice to be open about AI use; it is a soft disclosure recommendation (P24), worded as 'can help', so modality is should.
units.anchor: Being transparent about when and how you use AI tools, such as ChatGPT, can help
units.fit_note: Advisory; no required statement or format.

units.why: "AI is a powerful tool that can be used for learning, productivity, and creativity" names benefits of AI without making a rule, which is P87.
units.anchor: AI is a powerful tool that can be used for learning, productivity, and creativity.

units.why: "it is wise to avoid sharing any personal, confidential, or sensitive information" tells users to protect their data when AI tools store inputs, matching P50 (protect personal data).
units.anchor: it is wise to avoid sharing any personal, confidential, or sensitive information

units.why: "When AI is involved in your work ... it is helpful to let others know" recommends telling others which parts were AI-assisted; it adds a clarity-about-human-vs-AI rationale to P24 but is still disclosure.
units.anchor: When AI is involved in your work (whether writing, coding, analysis, or planning), it is
units.fit_note: Advisory, covers coding and analysis as well as writing; no format.

units.why: "AI can support your work, but it shouldn't replace thoughtful judgment or be used to mislead" says people should stay the decision-makers (P32) and not deceive (P74); I chose P32 as the main thought, the 'mislead' clause being a short add-on.
units.anchor: AI can support your work, but it shouldn’t replace thoughtful judgment or be used to
units.fit_note: Also says AI should not be used to mislead (P74).

units.why: "AI-generated content can also contain bias and error, so it is important to consider how this may affect your conclusions" tells users that output may be wrong or biased and must be weighed, which is P31.
units.anchor: AI-generated content can also contain bias and error, so it is important to consider how

units.why: "Staying curious and informed helps us all engage with these tools in more meaningful and responsible ways. Keep an eye out for learning opportunities" urges users to keep up with AI and training events (P102).
units.anchor: Keep an eye out for learning opportunities on campus and beyond.

units.why: "AI is evolving quickly, and so are our conversations about how to use it well. This site will continue to grow" says the guidance is provisional and will be updated (P54).
units.anchor: This site will continue to grow along with our community’s understanding and needs.

units.why: The page states "This site offers a starting point for exploring what AI is, how it's being used across campus, and what thoughtful, responsible use can look like", giving the purpose and scope of the university's AI site, i.e. a framework preamble (P56).
units.anchor: This site offers a starting point for exploring what AI is, how it’s being used

units.why: The page lists "Effective Date October 31, 2024" for the guidance, a statement of when it took effect, so P84.
units.anchor: Effective Date October 31, 2024
units.fit_note: Only a date; no process or body is named.

documents.summary: Faculty guidance from Writing in the Disciplines on how to set and communicate AI expectations in writing courses. It tells instructors to include a clear syllabus statement, gives sample statements for five levels from allowed to prohibited, and offers assignment-design and anti-cheating advice.
documents.stance_why: The page tells instructors that "each of us must specifically address AI" and offers sample statements headed "When AI is Generally Prohibited" and "When AI Use is Allowed with Prior Permission". It sets no stance of its own and hands the decision to instructors, so delegates with tiers.

units.why: "each of us must specifically address AI on multiple levels" tells instructors they must state AI expectations in course policy, assignments and assessment; it is an AI-statement requirement (P09), though framed as faculty guidance.
units.anchor: each of us must specifically address AI on multiple levels
units.fit_note: Guidance from a teaching unit, not a binding mandate.

units.why: "UVM's academic integrity policy requires us to be specific about our expectations" reports that instructors must be specific about AI, supporting P09 and noting that the Code's default 'may not address all questions'.
units.anchor: UVM’s academic integrity policy requires us to be specific about our expectations.

units.why: "Students report that the widespread lack of information about AI on syllabi creates confusion and uncertainty" is evidence for why syllabus statements are needed; it is student-reported evidence about AI practice (P55) not a rule.

units.anchor: We have options for weaving AI use and AI critical literacy into our assignments.

units.why: "Easy access to AI upends traditional approaches to assessment security" says AI undermines the reliability of assessments, matching P82 (limits of control).

documents.title: Understanding Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)
documents.summary: A student-facing writing center guide to generative AI. It tells students to follow their instructors' AI rules, restates the Code's default ban, explains limits and risks, and describes uses such as brainstorming, outlining, revising and citing, while steering students to writing tutors.
documents.stance_why: The guide says "pay attention to the policies your instructors have established in their courses" and "If you are not certain what the expectations are, check the syllabus and ask for guidance." It sets no rule of its own beyond quoting the Code, and hands the decision to instructors, so delegates.

units.why: "The purpose of this guide is to help you as a student writer to understand how GenAI works and to shape your decisions about whether, when, or how to use it" states the purpose of the guide and leaves the decision with students; P56 for purpose and scope.
units.anchor: to help you as a student writer to understand how GenAI works and to shape
units.fit_note: A guide's purpose statement, not an institutional framework.

units.why: "GenAI can mislead you and might get you into academic integrity trouble if you misuse it; however, when used strategically and appropriately, it can also help spark ideas, save time" lists benefits and risks; benefits of AI, P87.
units.anchor: when used strategically and appropriately, it can also help spark ideas, save time, support your

units.why: "It is better to use GenAI outputs as a starting place for your thinking ... rather than an endpoint and a tool rather than a crutch" tells students to stay the primary thinker, P32.
units.anchor: a starting place for your thinking, research, and exploration, rather than an endpoint
units.frag_end: a tool rather than a crutch.

units.why: "GenAI can't support the development of your writing processes as well as working with trained writing tutors" points students to human tutors alongside AI, P72.
units.anchor: Writing tutors can support you at all stages of your process
units.frag_end: even when you are also using GenAI!

units.why: "pay attention to the policies your instructors have established in their courses" tells students to follow each instructor's AI rules, P78.
units.anchor: pay attention to the policies your instructors have established in their courses

units.why: The guide quotes the Code: "Work generated by artificial intelligence is not considered to be created by the student and is not permitted unless expressly stated by the instructor." It restates the default ban unless the instructor allows, P06.
